psql -X dbname < dumpfile

where dumpfile is the file output by the pg_dump command. The database dbname will not be created by this command, so you must create it yourself from template0 before executing psql (e.g., with createdb -T template0 dbname). To ensure psql runs with its default settings, use the -X (--no-psqlrc) option. psql supports options similar to pg_dump for specifying the database server to connect to and the user name to use. See the psql reference page for more information.

Non-text file dumps should be restored using the pg_restore utility.

Before restoring an SQL dump, all the users who own objects or were granted permissions on objects in the dumped database must already exist. If they do not, the restore will fail to recreate the objects with the original ownership and/or permissions. (Sometimes this is what you want, but usually it is not.)

By default, the psql script will continue to execute after an SQL error is encountered. You might wish to run psql with the ON_ERROR_STOP variable set to alter that behavior and have psql exit with an exit status of 3 if an SQL error occurs:

psql -X --set ON_ERROR_STOP=on dbname < dumpfile

Either way, you will only have a partially restored database. Alternatively, you can specify that the whole dump should be restored as a single transaction, so the restore is either fully completed or fully rolled back. This mode can be specified by passing the -1 or --single-transaction command-line options to psql. When using this mode, be aware that even a minor error can rollback a restore that has already run for many hours. However, that might still be preferable to manually cleaning up a complex database after a partially restored dump.

The ability of pg_dump and psql to write to or read from pipes makes it possible to dump a database directly from one server to another, for example:

pg_dump -h host1 dbname | psql -X -h host2 dbname

Important

The dumps produced by pg_dump are relative to template0. This means that any languages, procedures, etc. added via template1 will also be dumped by pg_dump. As a result, when restoring, if you are using a customized template1, you must create the empty database from template0, as in the example above.

After restoring a backup, it is wise to run ANALYZE on each database so the query optimizer has useful statistics; see Section 24.1.3 and Section 24.1.6 for more information. For more advice on how to load large amounts of data into PostgreSQL efficiently, refer to Section 14.4.

25.1.2. Using pg_dumpall #

pg_dump dumps only a single database at a time, and it does not dump information about roles or tablespaces (because those are cluster-wide rather than per-database). To support convenient dumping of the entire contents of a database cluster, the pg_dumpall program is provided. pg_dumpall backs up each database in a given cluster, and also preserves cluster-wide data such as role and tablespace definitions. The basic usage of this command is:

pg_dumpall > dumpfile

The resulting dump can be restored with psql:

psql -X -f dumpfile postgres

(Actually, you can specify any existing database name to start from, but if you are loading into an empty cluster then postgres should usually be used.) It is always necessary to have database superuser access when restoring a pg_dumpall dump, as that is required to restore the role and tablespace information. If you use tablespaces, make sure that the tablespace paths in the dump are appropriate for the new installation.

pg_dumpall works by emitting commands to re-create roles, tablespaces, and empty databases, then invoking pg_dump for each database. This means that while each database will be internally consistent, the snapshots of different databases are not synchronized.

Cluster-wide data can be dumped alone using the pg_dumpall --globals-only option. This is necessary to fully backup the cluster if running the pg_dump command on individual databases.

25.1.3. Handling Large Databases #

Some operating systems have maximum file size limits that cause problems when creating large pg_dump output files. Fortunately, pg_dump can write to the standard output, so you can use standard Unix tools to work around this potential problem. There are several possible methods:

Use compressed dumps.  You can use your favorite compression program, for example gzip:

pg_dump dbname | gzip > filename.gz

Reload with:

gunzip -c filename.gz | psql dbname

or:

cat filename.gz | gunzip | psql dbname

Use split.  The split command allows you to split the output into smaller files that are acceptable in size to the underlying file system. For example, to make 2 gigabyte chunks:

pg_dump dbname | split -b 2G - filename

Reload with:

cat filename* | psql dbname

If using GNU split, it is possible to use it and gzip together:

pg_dump dbname | split -b 2G --filter='gzip > $FILE.gz'

It can be restored using zcat.

Use pg_dump's custom dump format.  If PostgreSQL was built on a system with the zlib compression library installed, the custom dump format will compress data as it writes it to the output file. This will produce dump file sizes similar to using gzip, but it has the added advantage that tables can be restored selectively. The following command dumps a database using the custom dump format:

pg_dump -Fc dbname > filename

A custom-format dump is not a script for psql, but instead must be restored with pg_restore, for example:

pg_restore -d dbname filename

See the pg_dump and pg_restore reference pages for details.

For very large databases, you might need to combine split with one of the other two approaches.

Use pg_dump's parallel dump feature.  To speed up the dump of a large database, you can use pg_dump's parallel mode. This will dump multiple tables at the same time. You can control the degree of parallelism with the -j parameter. Parallel dumps are only supported for the "directory" archive format.

pg_dump -j num -F d -f out.dir dbname

You can use pg_restore -j to restore a dump in parallel. This will work for any archive of either the "custom" or the "directory" archive mode, whether or not it has been created with pg_dump -j.

title: Local infrastructure overview
body:
Local infrastructure overview

Prepare before disconnecting

• Start the Docker engine on this Mac. Confirm it can run Linux arm64 containers.

• Open Infrastructure in Devline. Prepare only the services your project needs.

• Start each prepared service and wait for its readiness check. Open the service details to copy its actual host port, connection string, and generated credential.

• Prepare the project starter, SDK, and dependency cache separately. A database image cannot replace the application's compiler or packages.

• Open the service's offline reference and try the example while the engine is available.

The listed compressed sizes describe the selected platform's layers. The engine may reuse shared layers, and unpacked images and persistent data need additional disk space.

Set up a project in the terminal

Run these commands with a project directory that already exists. Prepare the pinned images while connected. The remaining commands use local files and the local Docker engine.

    devline infra catalog
    devline infra prepare postgres@18.6
    devline infra prepare rabbitmq@4.3.7
    devline infra configure ./my-app --service postgres@18.6 --service rabbitmq@4.3.7
    devline infra run ./my-app
    devline infra status --project ./my-app

Run devline infra credentials ./my-app in a private terminal when you need the generated passwords and connection strings. Run devline infra logs ./my-app to inspect startup. When finished, devline infra stop ./my-app stops the project services and keeps the named volumes.

Use the service offline

Starting a prepared service uses its cached image. Keep Docker's local VM running. Stop unused services to release their CPU and memory. A stopped service keeps its named volume, so restart the same instance to resume work. If the default port is busy, use a different loopback port and update the application's environment.

Devline's port mappings are for this Mac. Use 127.0.0.1 from an application running directly on macOS. A separate container has its own loopback interface. From Docker Desktop, use host.docker.internal for host-published ports when that route is available. For direct container-to-container traffic, connect both containers to the same user-defined Docker network and use the service's network name and container port. See application connections.

Know what you have

 Service   First task   Default host ports

 PostgreSQL   Test relational queries and transactions   5432

 MySQL   Test MySQL schemas and migrations   3306

 RabbitMQ   Publish and consume AMQP messages   5672, 15672

 Redis   Cache values and test expiry   6379

 MongoDB   Store JSON-like documents   27017

 NATS   Publish subjects and persist JetStream messages   4222, 8222

 Mailpit   Capture email without delivering it   1025, 8025

 Meilisearch   Index and search a local catalog   7700

 SeaweedFS S3   Upload and fetch objects over S3   8333

 Keycloak   Exercise OAuth and OpenID Connect flows   8180, 9100

Move a toolbox to another Mac

An image archive contains image layers and tags. The service's user data lives in its named volume. Save images and back up data separately, verify both on the destination, and keep credentials with a secure local copy of your project configuration. Follow image and data portability.

Troubleshooting

• A missing image means the selected service revision was never prepared on this engine or its cache was pruned.

• A failed readiness check often means initialization is still running, a volume belongs to an incompatible server version, or the app is using the wrong port. Read the container logs before replacing data.

• A service that is healthy but rejects your app connection usually needs the generated password, the correct database or virtual host, or the host name appropriate for where the app runs.

• Features that send mail, fetch remote identity providers, or call remote embedding models require a connection to those providers. Use local substitutes or disable those integrations for an offline session.

Docker volumes · Docker port publishing

title: Save images and back up service volumes
body:
Save images and back up service volumes

Move prepared images with Devline

The image vault is independent of Docker's cache. Transfer exact releases with a local vault archive, then load the verified images into Docker on the receiving Mac.

    devline infra export ./project-images.devlineinfra \
      --image postgres@18.6 --image redis@8.10.1
    shasum -a 256 ./project-images.devlineinfra

On the receiving Mac, compare the checksum, import the file, then restore the image into the local Docker engine.

    devline infra import ./project-images.devlineinfra
    devline infra verify postgres@18.6
    devline infra restore postgres@18.6

The vault contains service image archives. Install Docker, application runtimes, CLI tools, and project dependencies on the destination beforehand. Keep project credentials and any data volume backups separate.

Export images with Docker

Use the local image reference recorded by Devline or shown by docker image ls. If it is only in the vault, run devline infra restore postgres@18.6 first. The example adds a transport tag to a prepared PostgreSQL image. Replace IMAGE_ID with the exact local image ID displayed by docker image inspect for the prepared service.

    docker image inspect "$IMAGE_ID" --format '{{.Id}} {{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}'
    docker image tag "$IMAGE_ID" devline-offline/postgres:18.6
    docker image save -o devline-postgres-18.6-arm64.tar devline-offline/postgres:18.6
    shasum -a 256 devline-postgres-18.6-arm64.tar

On the receiving Mac, compare the archive SHA-256 with the separately recorded checksum, then load it.

    docker image load -i devline-postgres-18.6-arm64.tar
    docker image inspect devline-offline/postgres:18.6 --format '{{.Id}} {{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}'

Compare .Id with the catalog's image config digest. An image ID identifies the configuration of the platform image. The registry digest identifies the registry manifest. A local archive can preserve the image ID even when the engine does not retain the original registry manifest reference.

Run Compose from cached images

Point Compose at the actual local tag you saved and loaded. Set pull_policy: never and use the command-line pull guard. Supply the application's built image or dependencies separately.

    services:
      postgres:
        image: devline-offline/postgres:18.6
        platform: linux/arm64
        pull_policy: never
        environment:
          POSTGRES_DB: devline
          POSTGRES_USER: devline
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set a local password}
        ports:
          - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432"
        volumes:
          - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql
    volumes:
      pgdata:

    docker compose up --detach --pull never --no-build
    docker compose ps
    docker compose logs --tail 50 postgres

Inside this Compose network, a sibling app connects to postgres:5432. A macOS host app uses 127.0.0.1:5432. Keep generated passwords in a local file with restrictive permissions and exclude that file from version control.

Back up a named data volume

Use the database's logical export when available. For a cold copy, first stop the service and its writers. Determine the volume name from its managed container before removing anything.

    docker inspect "$CONTAINER" --format '{{range .Mounts}}{{println .Name .Destination}}{{end}}'
    docker stop "$CONTAINER"

Set VOLUME to the intended named volume and HELPER to a locally prepared Linux arm64 Alpine-based image containing tar. The catalog's Redis Alpine image works as the helper. Prepare it while connected, run devline infra restore redis@8.10.1 if needed, and get its local image reference from docker image ls. The helper has networking disabled and the source volume is read-only.

    docker run --rm --pull never --network none --entrypoint tar \
      --mount "type=volume,src=$VOLUME,dst=/source,readonly" \
      "$HELPER" -C /source -cf - . > service-data.tar
    shasum -a 256 service-data.tar
    docker start "$CONTAINER"

Restore into a fresh volume

Use the exact same image version and platform for a filesystem restore. Verify the archive's checksum and contents first. Use only an archive from a trusted source. Restore into a new empty volume and attach it to a new or stopped instance at the original mount path. Verify it before replacing the working service.

    tar -tf service-data.tar | head
    docker volume create devline-restored-data
    docker run --rm -i --pull never --network none --entrypoint tar \
      --mount type=volume,src=devline-restored-data,dst=/target \
      "$HELPER" -C /target -xpf - < service-data.tar

Keep the original instance until the restored database, queue, or object store passes its application smoke test. Preserve the same RabbitMQ node name when restoring its message store. Use service-specific tools for version upgrades.

title: Connect an application to local services
body:
Connect an application to local services

Keep endpoint settings in the app environment

Use the service details to copy the real mapped ports and credentials. These keys are examples your application can read from its environment. Store secrets in a local env file excluded from source control.

For a Devline-managed project, devline infra credentials ./my-app shows the resolved connection strings. The command intentionally reveals local credentials.

    DATABASE_URL=postgresql://devline:<password>@127.0.0.1:5432/devline
    AMQP_URL=amqp://devline:<password>@127.0.0.1:5672/devline
    REDIS_URL=redis://:<password>@127.0.0.1:6379/0
    SMTP_HOST=127.0.0.1
    SMTP_PORT=1025
    S3_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:8333
    S3_BUCKET=devline
    OIDC_ISSUER=http://127.0.0.1:8180/realms/devline

The variable names are application conventions. Match them to your framework or SDK. URL-encode characters in user info if you replace generated credentials with a password containing reserved characters. In a Compose application, use service names and internal ports. Match your configured OIDC issuer to the exact discovery URL used by your browser and application.

Make the database do real work

Set PG_CONTAINER to the running PostgreSQL container and execute a transaction using the client already installed in its image.

    docker exec -i "$PG_CONTAINER" psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U devline -d devline <<'SQL'
    BEGIN;
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS devline_probe (id integer PRIMARY KEY, note text NOT NULL);
    INSERT INTO devline_probe VALUES (1, 'offline')
    ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET note = EXCLUDED.note;
    SELECT id, note FROM devline_probe WHERE id = 1;
    ROLLBACK;
    SQL

Run the project's own migrations and integration tests next. They should use the same database URL the application receives.

Exercise a durable queue

Set RABBITMQ_PASSWORD to the generated broker credential and replace 15672 if you changed the management port. The management API can create, publish to, and read a disposable queue without an extra CLI or client package.

    base=http://127.0.0.1:15672/api
    curl -fsS -u "devline:$RABBITMQ_PASSWORD" -X PUT \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"durable":true}' \
      "$base/queues/devline/devline-probe"
    curl -fsS -u "devline:$RABBITMQ_PASSWORD" -X POST \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{"properties":{"delivery_mode":2},"routing_key":"devline-probe","payload":"offline","payload_encoding":"string"}' \
      "$base/exchanges/devline/amq.default/publish"
    curl -fsS -u "devline:$RABBITMQ_PASSWORD" -X POST \
      -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '{"count":1,"ackmode":"ack_requeue_false","encoding":"auto","truncate":1000}' \
      "$base/queues/devline/devline-probe/get"

Expect the publish response to contain "routed":true and the read response to contain the payload. Configure your app's AMQP library against the AMQP port and the same virtual host. The HTTP management endpoint is a useful probe. Application consumers should use AMQP acknowledgments and publishers should use confirms when delivery matters.

Plan for transport and startup

• Keep initialization, migration, and application startup as separate observable steps.

• A listening TCP port is not sufficient for an authenticated query. Use the service's readiness check before launching tests.

• A host port and container port can differ. For remote development or non-Docker-Desktop engines, test the actual route before going offline.

• Keep local credentials and example messages disposable. Do not copy data or access tokens into the repository.

title: PostgreSQL 18.6 · Local runbook
body:
PostgreSQL 18.6 · Local runbook

Image docker.io/library/postgres:18.6-alpine for Linux arm64. Default host ports 5432 for PostgreSQL.

Connect and query

Use the PostgreSQL URI from Devline's service details. The initial role and database are both devline. Set CONTAINER to the running container name. The image provides psql, pg_isready, pg_dump, and pg_restore.

    docker exec "$CONTAINER" pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U devline -d devline
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U devline -d devline \
      -c 'SELECT current_database(), current_user, version();'

If a host application cannot log in, compare its password and port with the service details. The direct container commands above use the local Unix socket for SQL. Check the application's authenticated TCP connection separately.

Persistence

The PostgreSQL 18 image stores its data under /var/lib/postgresql/18/docker. Devline mounts the named volume at /var/lib/postgresql. The bootstrap database, user, and password settings apply when the data directory is initialized. Changing the container environment alone does not update roles in an existing database.

Dump and restore

Create a custom-format dump while the service is running. Restore into a separate, empty database so you can inspect it before switching clients.

    docker exec "$CONTAINER" pg_dump -Fc -U devline -d devline > devline.pgdump
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" createdb -U devline -T template0 devline_restore
    docker exec -i "$CONTAINER" pg_restore --exit-on-error --no-owner \
      -U devline -d devline_restore < devline.pgdump
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" psql -X -U devline -d devline_restore -c '\dt'

A single-database dump excludes cluster roles and tablespaces. Use pg_dumpall --globals-only when those objects matter. Test restoration with the same or a compatible newer server version before replacing a project database.

title: MySQL 8.4.11 · Local runbook
body:
MySQL 8.4.11 · Local runbook

Image docker.io/library/mysql:8.4.11 for Linux arm64. Default host ports 3306 for MySQL.

Connect and query

Use the initial devline database and application user. The service has a separate root password for local administration. A cold first boot may take longer while MySQL initializes its data directory and creates the application grants.

    docker exec "$CONTAINER" sh -c 'exec mysql --host=127.0.0.1 --user=devline --password="$MYSQL_PASSWORD" --database=devline --execute="SELECT DATABASE(), CURRENT_USER(), VERSION()"'

Use an up-to-date MySQL 8.4 client or connector for the default authentication method. Change credentials through SQL for an existing volume. The initialization variables apply to a fresh data directory.

Dump and restore

For a consistent InnoDB snapshot, avoid schema changes during the dump. Use the root account inside the container and direct the dump to the Mac.

    docker exec "$CONTAINER" sh -c 'exec mysqldump --user=root --password="$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" --single-transaction --routines --events --no-tablespaces devline' > devline.mysql.sql
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" sh -c 'exec mysql --user=root --password="$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" --execute="CREATE DATABASE devline_restore"'
    docker exec -i "$CONTAINER" sh -c 'exec mysql --user=root --password="$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" devline_restore' < devline.mysql.sql
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" sh -c 'exec mysql --user=root --password="$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD" devline_restore --execute="SHOW TABLES"'

The dump contains application data. Keep it private and verify the restored schemas and rows before switching the project. Preserve the /var/lib/mysql volume when recreating the same service.

title: RabbitMQ 4.3.7 · Local runbook
body:
RabbitMQ 4.3.7 · Local runbook

Image docker.io/library/rabbitmq:4.3.7-management-alpine for Linux arm64. Default host ports 5672 for AMQP, 15672 for Management.

Connect and inspect

Use the AMQP URI from the service details. The application user and virtual host are devline. Open the management console on its host port, normally 15672, and use the same credentials. AMQP clients use port 5672 by default.

    docker exec "$CONTAINER" rabbitmq-diagnostics -q check_running
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" rabbitmq-diagnostics -q check_port_listener 5672
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" rabbitmqctl list_queues -p devline name durable messages

Use the application connections guide to publish and consume a test message.

Back up definitions

Definitions include topology, users, permissions, and policies. Treat the export as sensitive because it can contain password hashes.

    docker exec "$CONTAINER" rabbitmqctl export_definitions /tmp/rabbitmq-definitions.json
    docker cp "$CONTAINER:/tmp/rabbitmq-definitions.json" ./rabbitmq-definitions.json
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" rm /tmp/rabbitmq-definitions.json

On an isolated restore instance, copy the file in and import it. Verify its expected queues, exchanges, and vhosts before connecting applications.

    docker cp ./rabbitmq-definitions.json "$RESTORE_CONTAINER:/tmp/rabbitmq-definitions.json"
    docker exec "$RESTORE_CONTAINER" rabbitmqctl import_definitions /tmp/rabbitmq-definitions.json
    docker exec "$RESTORE_CONTAINER" rabbitmqctl list_vhosts

Definitions do not include messages. Stop the broker and take a cold copy of the entire /var/lib/rabbitmq volume for message persistence. Restore it with the same broker image and exactly the same Erlang node name.

title: Redis 8.10.1 · Local runbook
body:
Redis 8.10.1 · Local runbook

Image docker.io/library/redis:8.10.1-alpine for Linux arm64. Default host ports 6379 for Redis.

Connect and test expiry

Use the Redis URL from the service details. The image's local redis-cli receives the generated password through REDISCLI_AUTH.

    docker exec "$CONTAINER" redis-cli ping
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" redis-cli SET devline:probe offline EX 60
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" redis-cli GET devline:probe
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" redis-cli TTL devline:probe

A TTL of -2 means the key is absent. A TTL of -1 means the key exists without an expiry. Store cache prefixes and expirations explicitly in your app so local tests behave like the deployed cache.

Backup and restore

Devline enables the append-only file and mounts the /data volume. Inspect persistence before taking a copy.

    docker exec "$CONTAINER" redis-cli INFO persistence
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" redis-cli DBSIZE

Stop writes and use the cold volume backup for a local clone. Keep the whole data directory, including the append-only manifest and segments. Restore it into a fresh volume with the same Redis version, then verify PING, key count, and a known key. Redis prefers the AOF on restart when both AOF and an RDB snapshot are present.

Redis persistence · Redis CLI

title: MongoDB 8.0.34 · Local runbook
body:
MongoDB 8.0.34 · Local runbook

Image docker.io/library/mongo:8.0.34-noble for Linux arm64. Default host ports 27017 for MongoDB.

Connect and work with a document

The prepared instance is standalone. Use the connection URI from Devline, which authenticates the initial admin user against admin and selects the application database devline.

    docker exec "$CONTAINER" sh -c 'exec mongosh --quiet "mongodb://devline:$MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD@127.0.0.1:27017/devline?authSource=admin" --eval "db.probe.updateOne({id:1},{\$set:{value:\"offline\"}},{upsert:true}); printjson(db.probe.findOne({id:1}))"'

When testing application privileges, create a separate database-scoped user. The bootstrap credentials are for local administration. Test replica set transactions separately because a standalone instance does not exercise them.

Back up and restore

Use the MongoDB Database Tools inside the prepared container. The dump streams to a file on your Mac.

    docker exec "$CONTAINER" mongodump --version
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" sh -c 'exec mongodump --username=devline --password="$MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD" --authenticationDatabase=admin --db=devline --archive --gzip' > devline.mongo.archive
    docker exec -i "$CONTAINER" sh -c 'exec mongorestore --username=devline --password="$MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD" --authenticationDatabase=admin --archive --gzip --nsFrom="devline.*" --nsTo="devline_restore.*"' < devline.mongo.archive

Pause writers for a consistent logical copy of this standalone database. For a local clone, stop the server and use the cold volume backup on its /data/db volume and any configuration volume you use. Reopen with the same server version and verify a document read.

title: NATS 2.15.2 · Local runbook
body:
NATS 2.15.2 · Local runbook

Image docker.io/library/nats:2.15.2-alpine for Linux arm64. Default host ports 4222 for NATS, 8222 for HTTP monitoring.

Connect and monitor

Use the authenticated NATS URL from the service details. The client port is normally 4222. The monitoring port is normally 8222 and is intended for loopback inspection.

    curl -fsS 'http://127.0.0.1:8222/healthz?js-enabled-only=true'
    curl -fsS 'http://127.0.0.1:8222/varz'
    curl -fsS 'http://127.0.0.1:8222/jsz'

Core NATS delivers to live subscribers. Use JetStream for durable messages, replay, and consumer acknowledgments. With the optional NATS CLI already installed, use two terminals to smoke-test a subject.

    nats --server "$NATS_URL" sub devline.probe
    nats --server "$NATS_URL" pub devline.probe 'offline'

Persist and restore streams

JetStream uses the /data volume. The NATS CLI can take a stream snapshot and restore it to a compatible server. List the streams first so you can choose the right stream name.

    nats --server "$NATS_URL" stream ls
    nats --server "$NATS_URL" stream backup ORDERS ./orders-backup
    nats --server "$RESTORE_NATS_URL" stream restore ./orders-backup

Use a separate restore instance for testing. If the optional CLI is unavailable, stop the single-node server and copy its entire named volume using the cold volume backup. Restore using the same server version and check stream state and consumer behavior before moving application traffic.

title: Mailpit 1.33.0 · Local runbook
body:
Mailpit 1.33.0 · Local runbook

Image docker.io/axllent/mailpit:v1.33.0 for Linux arm64. Default host ports 1025 for SMTP, 8025 for Web inbox.

Capture a message

Configure the app to use SMTP at 127.0.0.1:1025 with local capture settings. The web inbox is at http://127.0.0.1:8025. Replace either port if you changed it in Devline.

    printf 'From: sender@example.test\r\nTo: recipient@example.test\r\nSubject: Offline probe\r\n\r\nMailpit captured this locally.\r\n' > mailpit-probe.eml
    curl -fsS --url smtp://127.0.0.1:1025 --mail-from sender@example.test \
      --mail-rcpt recipient@example.test --upload-file mailpit-probe.eml
    curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8025/readyz
    curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8025/api/v1/messages

Use the web inbox to inspect the HTML, plain text, headers, and attachments. The /api/v1/ page inside the local service includes its interactive API reference. Keep SMTP relay configuration disabled for local-only test mail.

Keep and move a test inbox

Devline stores the SQLite database at /data/mailpit.db with a 5,000-message retention limit. Stop the container before copying the volume so database sidecar files remain consistent. Use the cold volume backup and restore into a fresh volume at /data. Verify the message count after restart.

title: Meilisearch 1.56.1 · Local runbook
body:
Meilisearch 1.56.1 · Local runbook

Image docker.io/getmeili/meilisearch:v1.56.1 for Linux arm64. Default host ports 7700 for Search API.

Index and search a document

Use the HTTP endpoint and generated master key from the service details. Use the master key only in local administrative scripts. Give an app the narrower search key or scoped credentials it needs.

    base=http://127.0.0.1:7700
    curl -fsS "$base/health"
    curl -fsS -X POST "$base/indexes/devline/documents?primaryKey=id" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $MEILI_MASTER_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
      -d '[{"id":1,"title":"Offline search","tags":["local","reference"]}]'

The indexing response includes a taskUid. Read /tasks/<taskUid> using the same credential until it reports succeeded, then search.

    curl -fsS "$base/indexes/devline/search?q=offline" \
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $MEILI_MASTER_KEY"

Keyword search and local filtering run offline. An embedding setup that calls a remote provider needs that provider to be reachable.

Snapshot and restore

Request a snapshot and wait for the returned task to succeed. Copy the resulting file from the service's snapshots directory inside /meili_data.

    curl -fsS -X POST "$base/snapshots" -H "Authorization: Bearer $MEILI_MASTER_KEY"
    docker exec "$CONTAINER" ls -l /meili_data/snapshots

Use a fresh service directory and the same version to start Meilisearch with --import-snapshot /path/to/backup.snapshot. For a version migration, use a Meilisearch dump and follow the destination version's import procedure. A cold copy of /meili_data is another way to move a local instance at the same version.

title: SeaweedFS S3 4.52 · Local runbook
body:
SeaweedFS S3 4.52 · Local runbook

Image docker.io/chrislusf/seaweedfs:4.52 for Linux arm64. Default host ports 8333 for S3 API.

Connect to S3

This single-node mini deployment creates a devline bucket. Use the S3 endpoint and generated secret from Devline. Configure the SDK with access key devline, region us-east-1, and path-style addressing. The service endpoint is normally http://127.0.0.1:8333.

    curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8333/healthz
    printf 'offline object\n' > devline-probe.txt
    curl -fsS --aws-sigv4 'aws:amz:us-east-1:s3' \
      --user "devline:$AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" --upload-file devline-probe.txt \
      http://127.0.0.1:8333/devline/devline-probe.txt
    curl -fsS --aws-sigv4 'aws:amz:us-east-1:s3' \
      --user "devline:$AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" \
      http://127.0.0.1:8333/devline/devline-probe.txt

Use the generated secret in a local environment variable. If an SDK builds devline.127.0.0.1 instead of adding /devline to the endpoint path, set its force-path-style option.

Back up objects and metadata

A simple logical copy uses a prepared S3 client to download the bucket objects. This captures object contents. Use a cold copy of /data when you also need the local filer metadata, volume files, and mini configuration. Stop the service before copying. Restore the complete directory into a fresh volume and verify a signed request and a known object's contents.

  --user "devline:$AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" \

A simple logical copy uses a prepared S3 client to download the bucket objects. This captures object contents. title: Keycloak 26.8.2 · Local runbook
body:
Keycloak 26.8.2 · Local runbook

Image quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.8.2 for Linux arm64. Default host ports 8180 for Admin and OIDC, 9100 for Health.

Create a local realm and client

Open the Admin Console at http://127.0.0.1:8180 by default and use the bootstrap credentials shown in Devline. Create the devline realm, then add a client for your application's local callback URL. Use Authorization Code with PKCE for a browser or native public client. Set exact redirect URIs and web origins.

    curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:9100/health/ready
    curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8180/realms/devline/.well-known/openid-configuration

Use the issuer value from discovery in your app. A realm URL on localhost and one on 127.0.0.1 are different issuer strings. Keep the browser, SDK, and token validation settings consistent. Local dev mode and its embedded database are intended for local development.

Keep a development realm

The volume at /opt/keycloak/data holds the development database. For a local clone, stop Keycloak and copy the full named volume with the cold volume backup. Reopen with the same version and verify the realm's discovery and login.

For a logical realm export, use kc.sh export --realm devline --file /export/devline-realm.json in a stopped-server maintenance container using the same image and data volume. Import into a fresh instance using kc.sh import --file /export/devline-realm.json with that server stopped. Realm files can include client credentials and user details. Keep them out of the repository and review the export's user options.

title: SeaweedFS 4.52 · HTTP API
body:
SeaweedFS HTTP REST API

SeaweedFS exposes three HTTP surfaces:

 Service   Default port   Addressing

 Filer   8888   File system paths (/dir/name)

 Master   9333   File id assignment and cluster topology

 Volume server   8080   File content by file id (vid,fid)

Most clients only need the filer API (paths) or the S3 API. The master and volume APIs are the lower-level blob store interface.

Conventions applying to all three:

• Responses are JSON unless noted otherwise. Append &pretty=y to pretty-print.

• A file id (fid) has the form volumeId,fileKeyCookie, e.g. 3,01637037d6. An optional suffix selects a reserved id from a count assignment (3,01637037d6_1, _2, ...), and an optional extension (3,01637037d6.jpg) sets the content type on reads.

• replication is a 3-digit replica placement xyz: x copies in other data centers, y on other racks in the same data center, z on other volume servers on the same rack. 000 = no replication, 001 = one copy on the same rack, 010 = one copy on a different rack, 100 = one copy in another data center, 200 = two copies in two other data centers, 110 = one copy in another data center plus one on another rack.

• ttl units: m minute, h hour, d day, w week, M month, y year.

Filer API (port 8888)

The filer presents a POSIX-like namespace over the volume servers.

Upload a file

    # PUT the raw body to the target path
    curl -T /home/chris/myphoto.jpg "http://localhost:8888/dir/myphoto.jpg"

    # or POST as multipart form (the part filename becomes the entry name)
    curl -F file=@/home/chris/myphoto.jpg "http://localhost:8888/dir/"

Response 201 Created:

    {"name":"myphoto.jpg","size":43234,"eTag":"0x6c656...","mtime":"...","chunks":[...]}

Query parameters:

 Parameter   Description   Default

 collection   collection name   empty

 replication   replica placement code   filer default

 ttl   file expiration, e.g. 3d   never

 disk   disk type to store on   filer default

 fsync   true fsyncs on the volume server   false

 dataCenter   preferred data center   empty

 rack   preferred rack   empty

 dataNode   preferred volume server   empty

 saveInside   store small content inside the metadata instead of a volume   false

 maxMB   split the upload into chunks of this many MB   filer -maxMB

 mode   unix permission bits, e.g. 0644   0660

 op   append appends to an existing file   overwrite

 skipCheckParentDir   true skips the parent-directory existence check   false

Create a directory

    curl -X POST "http://localhost:8888/dir/newdir/"

A POST to a path ending in / with no content creates the directory, including missing parents.

Read a file

    curl "http://localhost:8888/dir/myphoto.jpg"

Supports Range requests (Accept-Ranges: bytes), ETag, and the If-None-Match / If-Modified-Since conditional headers. HEAD returns headers only. Entry headers stored as extended attributes are echoed back, minus internal Seaweed- and xattr- keys.

Entry metadata instead of content:

    curl "http://localhost:8888/dir/myphoto.jpg?metadata=true"

metadata=true&resolveManifest=true additionally resolves chunked-manifest entries into their real chunk list.

List a directory

    curl -H "Accept: application/json" "http://localhost:8888/dir/?limit=10&lastFileName=a.jpg"

 Parameter   Description   Default

 limit   max entries per page   filer -dirListLimit

 lastFileName   resume listing after this entry name   empty

 namePattern   include only names matching the wildcard   empty

 namePatternExclude   exclude names matching the wildcard   empty

The JSON response carries Path, Entries, Limit, LastFileName, ShouldDisplayLoadMore, and EmptyFolder. Without the Accept header the filer renders its HTML browser.

Move and copy

    curl -X POST "http://localhost:8888/dir/newname.jpg?mv.from=/dir/myphoto.jpg"
    curl -X POST "http://localhost:8888/dir/copy.jpg?cp.from=/dir/myphoto.jpg"

mv.from renames or moves the source to the request path (204 No Content). cp.from copies it.

Append

    curl -T chunk2.bin "http://localhost:8888/dir/file.bin?op=append"

Delete

    curl -X DELETE "http://localhost:8888/dir/myphoto.jpg"
    curl -X DELETE "http://localhost:8888/dir/?recursive=true"

 Parameter   Description   Default

 recursive   delete a non-empty directory tree   false; when the filer runs with filer.options.recursive_delete=true, deletes are recursive unless recursive=false

 ignoreRecursiveError   keep deleting remaining entries after an error   false

 skipChunkDeletion   remove only the metadata, keep volume data   false

Tagging

Tags are carried as Seaweed--prefixed request headers, not query parameters; ?tagging selects the tagging handler and ?tagging=K1,K2 lists the keys to remove. Header names are canonicalized on write (Seaweed-k1 is stored as Seaweed-K1), and the delete list is matched case-sensitively against the stored names.

    curl -X PUT -H "Seaweed-k1: v1" -H "Seaweed-k2: v2" "http://localhost:8888/dir/file.jpg?tagging"
    curl -X DELETE "http://localhost:8888/dir/file.jpg?tagging=K1,K2"

Read by file id

    curl "http://localhost:8888/?proxyChunkId=3,01637037d6"

The filer proxies the chunk read to the right volume server, so only the filer port needs to be exposed.

Resumable uploads

The filer serves the TUS protocol for resumable uploads (POST, PATCH, HEAD on upload URLs). It is enabled by default at /.tus; -tusBasePath changes the endpoint base path.

Health

GET /healthz and GET /readyz return 200 OK.

Master API (port 9333)

Write-affecting endpoints are automatically proxied to the current leader, so any master in the quorum can serve them.

Assign a file id

    curl "http://localhost:9333/dir/assign?count=1&replication=001&collection=turbo&dataCenter=dc1&ttl=3d&disk=ssd"
    {"count":1,"fid":"3,01637037d6","url":"127.0.0.1:8080","publicUrl":"localhost:8080"}

Upload the file content to http://<url>/<fid> afterwards. With count>1, use <fid>_1, <fid>_2, ... for the additional ids.

 Parameter   Description   Default

 count   file ids to reserve   1

 collection   collection name   empty

 dataCenter   preferred data center   empty

 rack   preferred rack   empty

 dataNode   preferred volume server   empty

 replication   replica placement   master -defaultReplication

 ttl   file expiration, e.g. 3d   never

 disk   disk type   empty

 dataSize   expected file size in bytes   0

 preallocate   bytes to preallocate for new volumes   master -volumePreallocate

 writableVolumeCount   grow this many volumes when none are writable   master default

 memoryMapMaxSizeMb   memory-mapped file size (Windows)   0

Look up a volume or file id

    curl "http://localhost:9333/dir/lookup?volumeId=3"
    {"locations":[{"url":"localhost:8080","publicUrl":"localhost:8080"}]}

 Parameter   Description   Default

 volumeId   volume id; a full vid,fid is accepted too   required

 fileId   like volumeId, but also returns a write JWT when security is on   empty

 collection   speeds up the lookup   empty

 read   yes generates a read JWT instead of a write JWT   empty

Store a file in one call

    curl -F file=@/home/chris/report.pdf "http://localhost:9333/submit?collection=turbo&replication=001"
    {"fileName":"report.pdf","fid":"3,01637037d6","fileUrl":"localhost:8080/3,01637037d6","size":43234,"eTag":"0x6c656..."}

POST /submit accepts multipart file data plus the dir/assign placement parameters (count, collection, dataCenter, rack, replication, ttl, disk), assigns a file id, uploads to the volume server, and returns the result.

Redirect to a file

    curl -v "http://localhost:9333/3,01637037d6"

GET /{fileId} answers 308 Permanent Redirect to a volume server holding the file, preserving the query string (e.g. image-resize parameters).

Cluster status

    curl "http://localhost:9333/dir/status?pretty=y"   # full topology tree
    curl "http://localhost:9333/vol/status?pretty=y"   # every volume on every node
    curl "http://localhost:9333/collection/info?collection=turbo"
    curl "http://localhost:9333/collection/info?collection=turbo&detail=true"

collection/info returns aggregated TotalSize, FileCount, UsedSize, VolumeCount; detail=true splits them per volume layout.

Grow volumes

    curl "http://localhost:9333/vol/grow?count=4&replication=001&collection=turbo&ttl=5d&disk=ssd&dataCenter=dc1&rack=rack1"
    {"count":4}

count is required; the placement parameters match dir/assign. One volume serves one write at a time, so pre-allocated volumes raise write concurrency.

Vacuum deleted space

    curl "http://localhost:9333/vol/vacuum?garbageThreshold=0.4"

 Parameter   Description   Default

 garbageThreshold   minimum deleted-bytes ratio before a volume is compacted   master -garbageThreshold (0.3)

Vacuuming makes a volume read-only, copies live needles to a new volume, and swaps it in.

Delete a collection

    curl "http://localhost:9333/col/delete?collection=benchmark"

Deletes all volumes of the collection, including erasure-coded shards. 204 No Content on success.

Health

    curl -I "http://localhost:9333/healthz"     # liveness
    curl -I "http://localhost:9333/readyz"      # readiness
    curl "http://localhost:9333/"               # web UI

Volume server API (port 8080)

The volume server stores file content by file id. Clients normally get the volume URL from dir/assign or dir/lookup.

Upload

    curl -F file=@/home/chris/myphoto.jpg "http://127.0.0.1:8080/3,01637037d6"
    {"name":"myphoto.jpg","size":43234,"eTag":"0x6c656...","mime":"image/jpeg","contentMd5":"..."}

PUT or POST the body (or a multipart file part) to /{vid},{fid}. 204 No Content is returned when the content is unchanged. ?ts=<unix> sets the stored modification time.

Read

    curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/3,01637037d6"
    curl "http://127.0.0.1:8080/3,01637037d6.jpg"        # sets Content-Type from the extension

Supports Range and HEAD. Image files can be resized server-side:

 Parameter   Description

 width, height   resize bounds in pixels

 mode   fit (contain) or fill (cover); omitted resizes to width/height

 crop_x1, crop_y1, crop_x2, crop_y2   explicit crop rectangle

 cm   false returns the chunk-manifest blob instead of resolving it

 readDeleted   true reads soft-deleted needles

 collection   passed through redirects for the right volume

Delete

    curl -X DELETE "http://127.0.0.1:8080/3,01637037d6"
    {"size":43234}

?ts=<unix> sets the deletion timestamp. Replicated volumes propagate the delete to every replica.

Status

    curl "http://localhost:8080/status?pretty=y"  # disk and volume inventory
    curl -I "http://localhost:8080/healthz"       # liveness/readiness

OPTIONS preflights answer CORS headers. When -port.public differs from -port, the volume server opens a separate read-only public listener on that port; -publicUrl sets the address it advertises to clients.
